# Use Alexa to Schedule Meetings and Hear Your Calendar Read Aloud by Voice

> **In short:** After linking Google, Outlook, or iCloud to the Alexa app, you can say "Alexa, what's on my calendar today?" to hear your day read aloud, and "Alexa, add a standup with the team at 10 AM tomorrow" to schedule a meeting — all hands-free. You need a calendar account, the free Alexa app, and either an Echo device or your phone.

Picture this: your hands are covered in flour from baking, you're in the middle of a workout, or you're already on a video call and can't reach your phone. That's exactly when a voice assistant earns its keep. This guide walks you through linking your calendar to Alexa and using simple spoken commands to add meetings and have your day read back to you — no typing, no tapping, no stopping what you're doing. A small honest note up front: Alexa is great at adding and reading basic events, but it can't reliably add attendees, send meeting invites, or handle complex recurring schedules — for those, you'll still want to open your calendar app.

## Before you start
- **An Amazon account** — the same one you use to shop on Amazon or watch Prime Video works fine.
- **The free Alexa app** on your phone (iOS or Android), **or** any Echo device such as an Echo Dot, Echo, or Echo Show.
- **A calendar account** — Google Calendar, Microsoft / Outlook (Office 365 or live.com), or Apple iCloud. The first two work best; iCloud setup is a bit more limited.
- **About 5–10 minutes** total the first time, mostly for signing in and approving the calendar link. After that, every voice command takes a few seconds.

## Step 1 — Link your calendar to Alexa
Open the Alexa app on your phone and tap the **More** tab at the bottom-right (three small lines or a grid icon). A menu slides up — scroll to **Settings** and tap it. Inside, look for a **Calendars** section (it may live under "Reminders" or "Lists & Notes" depending on your app version). Tap it, then tap **Add account** or the **+** button. Pick your provider — Google, Microsoft / Outlook, or Apple iCloud. A sign-in page opens in your browser; log in to your calendar account and approve the connection. A few seconds later, you'll bounce back to the Alexa app.
💬 Example: pick Google if your email ends in @gmail.com, or Microsoft if it ends in @outlook.com.
You'll know it worked when the Calendars screen lists your provider and email address (for example, "Google — yourname@gmail.com"). If nothing appears, sign in again — a typo in the password is the usual cause.

## Step 2 — Ask Alexa to read your day aloud
Say the wake word followed by a simple question. If you're near an Echo speaker, just say it out loud. If you're using the phone app, tap and hold the blue Alexa button at the bottom and speak. Alexa answers in plain English — no robotic list of fields, just a friendly walk through your day. The Echo's blue ring on top pulses while she listens and turns off when she's done. If she doesn't catch you the first time, try again more clearly or move closer.
💬 Example: "Alexa, what's on my calendar today?"
You'll know it worked when she starts naming your events one by one — "You have a standup at 10 AM, a call with Maria at 2 PM, and a dentist appointment at 4 PM." If she says "I don't see any events," check Step 1 — your calendar probably isn't linked yet.

## Step 3 — Add a meeting by voice
Now for the fun part — adding events without lifting a finger. Stand within range of your Echo (or hold the app button) and dictate the meeting. Include the **what**, **when**, and ideally the **who**. Be specific about the day — Alexa can get confused if you just say "at 10" without saying today or tomorrow. If the time is in the past, she'll ask you to confirm a future date. After you speak, she reads back what she understood before saving it.
💬 Example: "Alexa, add a standup with the team at 10 AM tomorrow."
You'll know it worked when she repeats the event back ("I've added a standup with the team tomorrow at 10 AM") and a new block appears in your linked calendar app within a few seconds.

## Step 4 — Add more details to an event
Once you've added the basic event, you can keep talking to flesh it out — duration, location, or notes. The trick is to mention the same event Alexa just created so she knows which one you mean. Names, days, and times are easy for her. Locations work if they're real places — "Conference Room B" or "the coffee shop on Main Street". Free-form notes are hit-and-miss: short phrases usually work, full sentences sometimes get cut off. If she mishears, just say "cancel that" and try again.
💬 Example: "Alexa, make it 30 minutes and add the location Conference Room B."
You'll know it worked when she confirms the change and the duration or location update shows up in your calendar app. If she asks a clarifying question instead, just answer it — "yes, tomorrow" or "no, the one on Friday."

## Step 5 — Check for time conflicts before adding
Voice-adding meetings is fast, which means it's also easy to double-book yourself. Before you confirm a new event, ask Alexa if that time slot is free. She'll check your linked calendar and tell you whether anything else is scheduled. This is a tiny habit that saves a lot of awkward "sorry, can we push that?" messages later. The check works for any time — past, present, or future.
💬 Example: "Alexa, am I free at 3 PM tomorrow?"
You'll know it worked when she answers "You don't have anything scheduled at 3 PM tomorrow" or names the event that's already there. If she says "I'm not sure," rephrase with a more specific time, like "3 in the afternoon on Thursday."

## Step 6 — Move, cancel, or reschedule by voice
Plans change — and Alexa can keep up. To change an existing event, just name it and say what you want done. She'll look up the matching event on your calendar and either update it or remove it. If you have two meetings at similar times, she may ask which one you mean — just answer with the detail she prompts for. Cancelled meetings stay deleted, but she can't tell your colleagues for you — for that, you'll still need to open your email or chat app.
💬 Example: "Alexa, move my 3 PM meeting to 4 PM" or "Alexa, cancel my dentist appointment."
You'll know it worked when she confirms the change — "I've moved your 3 PM meeting to 4 PM" — and you see the update reflected in your calendar app within a few seconds.

## Common mistakes
- **Skipping the calendar link.** If you skip Step 1, every command after this will fail silently — Alexa will say "I don't see any events" or add the meeting to her internal list instead of your real calendar. **Fix:** open the app and link an account before trying again.
- **Being vague about the day.** Saying "add a meeting at 2" leaves Alexa guessing between today, tomorrow, and next week. **Fix:** always include the day, like "at 2 PM on Friday" or "tomorrow at 2".
- **Expecting Alexa to invite people.** She can add event titles that mention teammates, but she can't actually email attendees or send meeting invites from her own voice. **Fix:** open your calendar app after the event is created to add guests and the video-call link manually.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** while cooking, doing the dishes, or carrying a child on your hip, you can add a school pickup reminder or check tomorrow's appointments without touching your phone — your day stays in your head instead of on a locked screen.
- **For your business or work:** during back-to-back meetings, a quick "Alexa, what's next on my calendar?" lets you see what's coming without breaking eye contact or opening a laptop — and "Alexa, schedule a follow-up with marketing for Friday at 11" gets the appointment booked while you stay focused on the call in front of you.
- **If you're just getting started:** the easiest first move is the very next time you're near your Echo or have the app open — just say "Alexa, what's on my calendar today?" and listen. That's it.

## Try it now
Walk up to any Echo in your home (or open the Alexa app), and say exactly this: **"Alexa, what's on my calendar today?"** Then listen. You'll either hear your day read back to you — which is a small, satisfying moment — or you'll find out right away that you need to follow Step 1 to link a calendar first. Either way, you'll know where you stand, and the rest of this guide will make sense.
